indri

Estimates the additive genetic covariance matrix G (traits × traits) for large trait sets, without fitting one giant multivariate animal model.

It does this LiMMBo’s way: split the traits into many small, overlapping subsets, fit a small animal model on each, and reassemble the estimates into a single positive semi-definite matrix. The per-subset fit is pluggable, so the same estimator runs on a Bayesian sampler or on a REML engine, and every engine comes with per-entry uncertainty. See the LiMMBo paper.

The assembled G, with the residual covariance E (the residual covariance of Y after X minus G), then drives genome-wide association scans: one multi-trait test per SNP across all the traits, or trait-by-trait tests, in a linear mixed model, with optional dominance effects (indri_gwas(), below).

Status (0.4.0): working and validated on simulations of up to 35 traits; association scans calibrated at 10 and 30 traits; genotype-by-environment scans (experimental) mildly conservative. The assembled G is as accurate as the full model where the full model can be fitted; the 95% bands cover the true correlations about 95-97% of the time. See STATUS.md for the numbers.

Install 

remotes::install_github("diogro/indri", subdir = "package")

You also need at least one block engine:

Engine Package Needs Uncertainty
"stanimal" (default) stanimal (>= 0.8.0 recommended) CmdStan posterior draws
"sommer" sommer REML sampling distribution
"asreml" ASReml-R a licence (one seat per worker) REML sampling distribution

Every engine accepts gaps (NA) in Y and uses each individual’s observed traits. stanimal gives a posterior; the REML engines are much faster for large N.

Quick start 

library(indri)
set.seed(1)

# A known 6-trait genetic covariance on a sibship design.
G_true <- stanimal::random_covariance(
  n_traits = 6, method = "partial", min_var = 0.8, max_var = 1.4
)
E_true <- stanimal::random_covariance(
  n_traits = 6, method = "lkj", lkj_prior = 2, min_var = 0.5, max_var = 0.9
)
A <- kronecker(diag(20), matrix(0.5, 8, 8))
diag(A) <- 1
Y <- t(chol(A)) %*% matrix(stats::rnorm(nrow(A) * 6), nrow(A), 6) %*% chol(G_true) +
     matrix(stats::rnorm(nrow(A) * 6), nrow(A), 6) %*% chol(E_true)
colnames(Y) <- paste0("trait", 1:6)

fit <- fit_G(
  Y, A = A, engine = "stanimal",
  engine_args = list(chains = 1, iter = 600, refresh = 0, show_messages = FALSE)
)

fit                                            # summary print
fit$G                                          # G, in the units of Y
fit$corrG                                      # genetic correlations
apply(fit$corrG_draws, 1:2, quantile, 0.975)   # per-entry upper 95% bound

Fixed effects go in a design matrix with one row per individual, which must include an intercept (or every level of a factor). stanimal’s animal_design() builds all three inputs from a formula, a data frame and a pedigree:

d <- stanimal::animal_design(cbind(t1, t2, t3) ~ sex + age, data = dat,
                             pedigree = ped)
fit <- fit_G(d$Y, X = d$X, A = d$A)

What you get back

slot what it is
G, corrG, sigma_G the assembled estimate (G and sigma_G in the units of Y)
G_draws, corrG_draws assembled draws (traits × traits × draws), for per-entry intervals
G_bar the average of the blocks before the PSD projection
E, E_bar the residual covariance for association scans (residual covariance of Y after X minus G, kept well conditioned; units of Y), and the average of the block residual covariances
subsets, coverage the trait subsets fitted, and how many covered each pair
diagnostics per-block convergence; uncertified blocks listed by trait
blocks the raw block fits, on the internal standardised scale
y_mean, y_sd that standardisation

print(), summary() and plot() are provided. A progress bar of the block fits shows in interactive sessions (progress = TRUE forces it).

Association scans

indri_gwas() tests SNPs against the traits. The multi-trait test is the reason to estimate G and E for many traits at once: it tests each SNP against all of them jointly, in a mixed model whose covariance is G and E with the relationship matrix A.

fit <- fit_G(Y, X = X, A = A)                  # G and E, once
scan <- indri_gwas(Y, genotypes, fit = fit, A = A, X = X,
                   snp_info = snp_info)        # one test per SNP, all traits
scan                                           # summary print
summary(scan)                                  # top SNPs, genomic inflation
plot(scan)                                     # Manhattan plot (ggplot2)
plot(scan, type = "qq")                        # QQ plot
head(as.data.frame(scan))                      # one row per SNP, for write.csv()

# trait by trait, adjusted for the effective number of traits
single <- indri_gwas(Y, genotypes, A = A, X = X, mode = "single_trait",
                     adjust = "effective")

# additive and dominance effects
dom <- indri_gwas(Y, genotypes, fit = fit, A = A, X = X, dominance = TRUE)

genotypes is an individuals × SNPs matrix (typically 0/1/2); samples are matched to Y, A and X by row name. snp_info is an optional data frame (for example snp, chrom, pos) carried into the results.

mode, model test per SNP covariance
"multi_trait", "lmm" (default) joint, P degrees of freedom G ⊗ A + δ E ⊗ I
"multi_trait", "lm" joint, P degrees of freedom E ⊗ I, E the residual covariance after X
"single_trait", "lmm" one per trait A + δ I per trait, δ by REML or from the fit
"single_trait", "lm" one per trait ordinary least squares

Every test is a likelihood ratio with the overall scale profiled. The covariance is diagonalised once, so a scan costs one N × N rotation of the genotypes plus O(N P) per SNP: thousands of SNPs take seconds.

  • delta. G and E set the shape of the covariance; the ratio δ between them is re-fitted once under the null (no SNP) and held fixed for every SNP. With a G and E from the same data it comes out near 1, and it is returned (scan$delta) so that you can check. A value far from 1 says the covariances do not describe the data being scanned; the test stays calibrated either way. Pass delta = to fix it instead.
  • Dominance. dominance = TRUE adds a heterozygote indicator next to each SNP’s dosage: pvalues becomes the joint additive + dominance test, pvalues_dominance tests dominance given the additive effect, and a and d are the additive and dominance effects (Falconer’s symbols). It needs genotypes coded 0/1/2 and all three genotypes in numbers: a SNP seen in only two genotype classes keeps the additive test and gets NA dominance results (dominance_estimable).
  • Genotype by environment. gxe = "sex" (any columns of X) adds each SNP’s interaction with those environments: pvalues becomes the joint test of the SNP and its interactions, pvalues_gxe tests the interactions given the main effect, and gxe holds their effects. GxE in the background (a polygenic G x E, or residual variance differing between environments) is not modelled by default: pass a fit_G_env() fit (experimental) as fit for a background with its own G in each environment and between environments. That removes the inflation, but fit_G_env() currently underestimates cross-environment genetic correlations, so its interaction tests are conservative.
  • Permutations. n_permutations reruns the scan with the genotypes permuted across individuals: pvalues_empirical per SNP, and qvalues_empirical, the permutation estimate of the false discovery rate. With fdr = 0.05, fdr_threshold is the p-value at or below which SNPs are discoveries at that rate. Permuting across relatives ignores their relatedness, so treat these as a check on the analytic p-values.
  • Adjusting single-trait p-values for the number of traits: adjust = "bonferroni" multiplies by the number of traits, "effective" by the effective number of independent traits (Galwey 2009, indri_effective_tests()), counted on the residuals after X.
  • Inputs. Y must be complete. Missing genotypes are replaced by the SNP’s mean; monomorphic SNPs get NA with a warning. The mixed models need A; the multi-trait one needs G and E, from fit or given directly.
slot what it is
pvalues one per SNP (multi-trait) or SNP × trait (single-trait)
a additive effects, SNP × trait, in the units of Y per allele
delta the null variance ratio (one, or one per trait)
pvalues_dominance, d, dominance_estimable with dominance = TRUE
pvalues_gxe, gxe, gxe_estimable with gxe
pvalues_adjust, n_tests with adjust
pvalues_empirical, qvalues_empirical, fdr_threshold with n_permutations (and fdr)
snp_info the SNP information, or the SNP names

indri_locus_G(scan, genotypes = genotypes) turns the loci’s a and d into the additive and dominance covariance matrices they imply, with the allele frequencies and linkage disequilibrium of the genotypes (Melo, Marroig and Wolf 2019): how the mapped loci build up the genetic covariance between traits.

Data. The package ships an F3 intercross of the LG/J and SM/J mouse strains: lgsm_f3 (1611 mice; growth (weekly gains), raw weekly weight, mandible area and necropsy traits, listed in lgsm_traits), lgsm_genotypes (353 markers coded additive A, dominance D and imprinting I; A + 1 is the 0/1/2 dosage indri_gwas() takes; data from Melo, Marroig and Wolf 2019, doi:10.1093/jhered/esz011), lgsm_markers (the map), and lgsm_pedigree and lgsm_A (the F3 relationship matrix; the F2 parents are unrelated founders, as the P strains are inbred and the F1 all heterozygous).

examples/gwas.R runs the whole pipeline on simulated sibs in under a minute, with four planted SNPs showing where each test is strongest, permutations, and the plots.

Caveats worth knowing

  • Intervals are per entry. The draws are assembled from dependent blocks: use them for intervals on individual covariances and correlations, not for functions of the whole matrix (eigenvalues, integration). Measured coverage at nominal 95%: 0.96-0.98 for the REML engines, about 0.95 for stanimal.
  • Strong correlations are shrunk a little, so integration is understated rather than overstated: the eigenvalue variance of corrG came out at about 75-85% of the truth’s at 35 traits.
  • Blocks are small by default: up to four traits each, every pair in three distinct blocks for stanimal (fitted with lkj_prior = 1) and in at least one for the REML engines. Larger blocks shrank stanimal’s correlations and gave the REML engines nothing for their cost.
  • asreml needs a licence seat per worker. It runs two workers by default; a standard licence allows two processes on one machine at a time. Use cores = 1 with a single seat.
  • Units. G is in the units of Y since 0.2.0; fits saved by 0.1.0 hold a standardised G.
  • Association scans condition on the point estimates of G and E; their uncertainty is not propagated. Fits made before E was assembled need refitting to drive the multi-trait test. Genotypes are read as matrices only (no PLINK reader).

Vignettes

Four worked analyses of the nine weekly weight gains of the LG/SM F3 mice (lgsm_f3), precomputed (the fits take up to half an hour), and online at https://diogro.github.io/indri/:

  • Estimating G for many traits: engines and priors: sommer, asreml and stanimal on the same data, reading a fit, choosing the LKJ prior, and G against P.
  • Genome scans for many traits: multi- and single-trait scans, thresholds and permutations, dominance, effects across the growth curve.
  • G from locus effects: indri_locus_G() on the mapped loci, compared with the polygenic G.
  • Genotype-by-environment scans: genetic covariance within and between the sexes, and interaction scans with two backgrounds.

browseVignettes("indri") lists them once the package is installed with its vignettes. The site is a pkgdown site in docs/, with this README as its home page: rebuild it with Rscript package/pkgdown/build_site.R after precompute.R.

Repository map

  • NOTES.md: design, engine contract and the reasons for the defaults.
  • STATUS.md: what has been measured and what comes next.
  • AGENTS.md: guidance for coding agents working on the package.
  • examples/: worked examples, including the genome scan in gwas.R.
  • GWAS_PLAN.md: the association-testing port from LiMMBo, its decisions and what remains.

Scope

In scope: G and E from a phenotype matrix Y, a design X and a known relationship matrix A, and association scans that use them. Out of scope for now: P and h2 reporting, breeding values, imputation, model comparison.

Reference

Meyer, H. V., Casale, F. P., Stegle, O., and Birney, E. (2018). LiMMBo: a simple, scalable approach for linear mixed models in high-dimensional genetic association studies. bioRxiv, preprint. https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/255497v1
